claim: In noisy settings, listening is aided by correlated dynamic visual cues gleaned from a talker's face.
source: In noisy settings, listening is aided by correlated dynamic visual cues gleaned from a talker's face—an improvement often attributed to visually reinforced linguistic information.
evidence: This is a general statement about audio-visual speech perception that is part of established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Performance improved when the auditory target's timecourse matched that of the visual stimulus.
source: Performance improved when the auditory target's timecourse matched that of the visual stimulus.
evidence: This is the main experimental finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the results section.

claim: The coherence was between task-irrelevant stimulus features.
source: The fact that the coherence was between task-irrelevant stimulus features suggests that the observed improvement stemmed from the integration of auditory and visual streams into cross-modal objects, enabling listeners to better attend the target.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The observed improvement stemmed from the integration of auditory and visual streams into cross-modal objects.
source: The fact that the coherence was between task-irrelevant stimulus features suggests that the observed improvement stemmed from the integration of auditory and visual streams into cross-modal objects, enabling listeners to better attend the target.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on inference from the data.

claim: Temporal cues provided by vision can help listeners to select one sound source from a mixture in everyday conditions where listeners can see the source of a sound.
source: These findings suggest that in everyday conditions, where listeners can often see the source of a sound, temporal cues provided by vision can help listeners to select one sound source from a mixture.
evidence: This is a generalization of the experimental findings to real-world scenarios, based on inference from the data.

claim: Auditory scene analysis underlies our ability to listen to one sound while ignoring others and is crucial for everyday listening.
source: This process of auditory scene analysis underlies our ability to listen to one sound while ignoring others and is crucial for everyday listening.
evidence: This is established knowledge in auditory neuroscience.

claim: Psychophysical studies have focused on the perceptual 'rules' that govern the likelihood of elements being grouped into single objects in audition.
source: While psychophysical studies have focused on the perceptual 'rules' that govern the likelihood of elements being grouped into single objects in audition (Bregman, 1990; Bizley and Cohen, 2013) or in vision (Marr, 1982; Lee and Yuille, 2006), perception is a seamlessly multisensory process whereby sensory information is integrated both within and across different sensory modalities.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Perception is a seamlessly multisensory process whereby sensory information is integrated both within and across different sensory modalities.
source: While psychophysical studies have focused on the perceptual 'rules' that govern the likelihood of elements being grouped into single objects in audition (Bregman, 1990; Bizley and Cohen, 2013) or in vision (Marr, 1982; Lee and Yuille, 2006), perception is a seamlessly multisensory process whereby sensory information is integrated both within and across different sensory modalities.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of multisensory perception.

claim: There has yet to be a study utilizing ongoing, continuous stimuli that demonstrates a perceptual benefit of an uninformative visual stimulus when selectively attending to one auditory stimulus in a mixture.
source: To date, there has yet to be a study utilizing ongoing, continuous stimuli that demonstrates a perceptual benefit of an uninformative visual stimulus when selectively attending to one auditory stimulus in a mixture.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the literature, which can be verified through review of existing studies.

claim: When listening in a noisy setting, watching a talker's face drastically improves speech intelligibility.
source: When listening in a noisy setting, watching a talker's face drastically improves speech intelligibility (Binnie, 1973; Bernstein and Grant, 2009) and this benefit is particularly apparent under difficult listening conditions, such as when speech is masked by spatially coincident competing speech (Helfer and Freyman, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The benefit of watching a talker's face is particularly apparent under difficult listening conditions, such as when speech is masked by spatially coincident competing speech.
source: When listening in a noisy setting, watching a talker's face drastically improves speech intelligibility (Binnie, 1973; Bernstein and Grant, 2009) and this benefit is particularly apparent under difficult listening conditions, such as when speech is masked by spatially coincident competing speech (Helfer and Freyman, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The unvoiced consonants /p/, /t/, and /k/ can be disambiguated based upon mouth movements.
source: Much work has focused on the role that visual information plays in contributing linguistic information—for example, the unvoiced consonants /p/, /t/, and /k/ can be disambiguated based upon mouth movements, a fact which underlies the McGurk effect whereby conflicting acoustic and visual information create an intermediary percept, changing which syllable a listener hears (McGurk and MacDonald, 1976).
evidence: This is established knowledge in speech perception, supported by citation.

claim: The McGurk effect occurs when conflicting acoustic and visual information create an intermediary percept, changing which syllable a listener hears.
source: Much work has focused on the role that visual information plays in contributing linguistic information—for example, the unvoiced consonants /p/, /t/, and /k/ can be disambiguated based upon mouth movements, a fact which underlies the McGurk effect whereby conflicting acoustic and visual information create an intermediary percept, changing which syllable a listener hears (McGurk and MacDonald, 1976).
evidence: This is a well-known phenomenon in speech perception, supported by citation.

claim: Benefits of visual information for speech perception are specific to speech signals.
source: Such benefits are specific to speech signals, however, leaving questions about the general principles that govern multisensory integration and its perceptual benefits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review presented in the introduction.

claim: When performing simple tone-in-noise detection, thresholds improve when the timing of the potential tone is unambiguous.
source: When performing simple tone-in-noise detection, thresholds improve when the timing of the potential tone is unambiguous (Watson and Nichols, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Visual speech cues precede the auditory signal.
source: Visual speech cues, which precede the auditory signal (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009; Stevenson et al., 2012), provide helpful information about when to listen (Grant and Seitz, 2000; Grant, 2001; Bernstein et al., 2004) and may help target speech to be separated from other competing speech (Summerfield, 1992; Devergie et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual speech cues provide helpful information about when to listen.
source: Visual speech cues, which precede the auditory signal (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009; Stevenson et al., 2012), provide helpful information about when to listen (Grant and Seitz, 2000; Grant, 2001; Bernstein et al., 2004) and may help target speech to be separated from other competing speech (Summerfield, 1992; Devergie et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual speech cues may help target speech to be separated from other competing speech.
source: Visual speech cues, which precede the auditory signal (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009; Stevenson et al., 2012), provide helpful information about when to listen (Grant and Seitz, 2000; Grant, 2001; Bernstein et al., 2004) and may help target speech to be separated from other competing speech (Summerfield, 1992; Devergie et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and involves some speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Temporal coherence may facilitate binding of auditory and visual stimuli into single cross-modal objects.
source: In addition to information about when to listen, timing may be important for another reason: temporal coherence may facilitate binding of auditory and visual stimuli into single cross-modal objects.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on inference from existing knowledge.

claim: Previous studies of audio–visual binding have focused on judgments of coherence or simultaneity rather than on the perceptual enhancements provided by that binding.
source: However, previous studies of audio–visual binding—the integration of auditory and visual stimuli into a single percept—have focused on judgments of coherence or simultaneity (Recanzone, 2003; Spence and Squire, 2003; Fujisaki and Nishida, 2005; Denison et al., 2013), rather than on the perceptual enhancements provided by that binding.
evidence: This is a characterization of the literature supported by citations.

claim: A sound can affect the perceived number of visual stimuli.
source: A sound can affect the perceived number of visual stimuli (Shams et al., 2000, 2002; Bizley et al., 2012), the color (Mishra et al., 2013), and the direction of visual motion (Freeman and Driver, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A sound can affect the perceived color of visual stimuli.
source: A sound can affect the perceived number of visual stimuli (Shams et al., 2000, 2002; Bizley et al., 2012), the color (Mishra et al., 2013), and the direction of visual motion (Freeman and Driver, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A sound can affect the perceived direction of visual motion.
source: A sound can affect the perceived number of visual stimuli (Shams et al., 2000, 2002; Bizley et al., 2012), the color (Mishra et al., 2013), and the direction of visual motion (Freeman and Driver, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A task-irrelevant sound can increase detection of a visual stimulus.
source: A task-irrelevant sound can also increase detection of a visual stimulus (McDonald et al., 2000) by affecting the bias and sensitivity, as well as alter the perceived visual intensity (Stein et al., 1996; Odgaard et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A task-irrelevant sound can alter the perceived visual intensity.
source: A task-irrelevant sound can also increase detection of a visual stimulus (McDonald et al., 2000) by affecting the bias and sensitivity, as well as alter the perceived visual intensity (Stein et al., 1996; Odgaard et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: An irrelevant visual stimulus can affect the detection of an auditory stimulus.
source: Similarly, an irrelevant visual stimulus can affect the detection of an auditory stimulus (Lovelace et al., 2003) as well as the perceived loudness (Odgaard et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: An irrelevant visual stimulus can affect the perceived loudness of an auditory stimulus.
source: Similarly, an irrelevant visual stimulus can affect the detection of an auditory stimulus (Lovelace et al., 2003) as well as the perceived loudness (Odgaard et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Previous studies have not demonstrated benefits of cross-modal effects when segregating streams.
source: These effects could all conceivably help when segregating streams, but none of these studies demonstrated such benefits.
evidence: This is a characterization of the literature based on review of previous studies.

claim: The study developed a novel paradigm designed to test whether cross-modal temporal coherence was sufficient to promote the segregation of two competing sound sources.
source: In this study, we developed a novel paradigm that was designed to test whether cross-modal temporal coherence was sufficient to promote the segregation of two competing sound sources.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The study manipulated temporal coherence in an ethologically relevant modulation frequency range.
source: We chose to manipulate temporal coherence in an ethologically relevant modulation frequency range (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009), amplitude modulating our stimuli with a noisy envelope low-pass filtered at 7 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design with citation support for the frequency range choice.

claim: The stimuli were amplitude modulated with a noisy envelope low-pass filtered at 7 Hz.
source: We chose to manipulate temporal coherence in an ethologically relevant modulation frequency range (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009), amplitude modulating our stimuli with a noisy envelope low-pass filtered at 7 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The authors hypothesized that modulating the visual stimulus coherently with one of the auditory streams would cause these stimuli to automatically bind together.
source: We hypothesized that modulating the visual stimulus coherently with one of the auditory streams would cause these stimuli to automatically bind together, with a consequent improvement in performance when the visual stimulus was coherent with the target auditory stream.
evidence: This is the stated hypothesis of the study.

claim: The authors hypothesized that binding would result in an improvement in performance when the visual stimulus was coherent with the target auditory stream.
source: We hypothesized that modulating the visual stimulus coherently with one of the auditory streams would cause these stimuli to automatically bind together, with a consequent improvement in performance when the visual stimulus was coherent with the target auditory stream.
evidence: This is the stated hypothesis of the study.

claim: The visual stimulus itself provided no additional information about the timing of the target auditory perturbations.
source: Importantly, any perceptual benefit could only result from the temporal coherence between the auditory and visual stimulus, as the visual stimulus itself provided no additional information about the timing of the target auditory perturbations.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: All methods were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Washington and the Ethics Committee of the University College London.
source: All methods were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Washington and the Ethics Committee of the University College London (ref: 5139).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: The visual stimulus was uninformative of the auditory task.
source: Importantly, the visual stimulus was uninformative of the auditory task, such that any behavioral benefit could be unambiguously determined to be the result of selective enhancement of an auditory stream due to binding with the visual stimulus.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The temporal dynamics of each stream were defined by low-pass noise envelopes with a 7 Hz cutoff frequency.
source: The temporal dynamics of each stream were defined by low-pass noise envelopes with a 7 Hz cutoff frequency, roughly approximating the modulation frequency range of speech amplitude envelopes and visual mouth movements (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The 7 Hz cutoff frequency roughly approximates the modulation frequency range of speech amplitude envelopes and visual mouth movements.
source: The temporal dynamics of each stream were defined by low-pass noise envelopes with a 7 Hz cutoff frequency, roughly approximating the modulation frequency range of speech amplitude envelopes and visual mouth movements (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Each trial was 14 s in duration.
source: In each trial of 14 s duration there were two auditory streams (one target, one masker; Figure 1A) that were amplitude-modulated by independent tokens of the noise envelope and one visual stream: a gray disc surrounded by a white ring whose radius was also modulated by a noise envelope (envelope in Figure 1B; images of disc in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: There were two auditory streams (one target, one masker) in each trial that were amplitude-modulated by independent tokens of the noise envelope.
source: In each trial of 14 s duration there were two auditory streams (one target, one masker; Figure 1A) that were amplitude-modulated by independent tokens of the noise envelope and one visual stream: a gray disc surrounded by a white ring whose radius was also modulated by a noise envelope (envelope in Figure 1B; images of disc in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The visual stream consisted of a gray disc surrounded by a white ring whose radius was modulated by a noise envelope.
source: In each trial of 14 s duration there were two auditory streams (one target, one masker; Figure 1A) that were amplitude-modulated by independent tokens of the noise envelope and one visual stream: a gray disc surrounded by a white ring whose radius was also modulated by a noise envelope (envelope in Figure 1B; images of disc in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods with reference to Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: The visual radius envelope could match the amplitude envelope of the target auditory stream, the masker auditory stream, or be independent from both.
source: The visual radius envelope could match the amplitude envelope of the target auditory stream (example stimuli in Video 1) or masker auditory stream (Video 2), or be independent from both (Video 3).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions with reference to Videos 1-3.

claim: The three experimental conditions were referred to as match-target, match-masker, and match-neither.
source: This audio–visual coherence (specifically which, if either, auditory stream's amplitude envelope was matched by the visual radius) defined the three experimental conditions, henceforth referred to as match-target, match-masker, and match-neither, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The goal of the subject was to respond by pressing a button to brief perturbation events in the target stream and ignore events in the masker stream.
source: The goal of the subject was to respond by pressing a button to brief perturbation events in the target stream and ignore events in the masker stream.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: The task-relevant auditory feature was not the same feature that was coherent with the visual stimulus.
source: Importantly, the task-relevant auditory feature was not the same feature that was coherent with the visual stimulus.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: A response to an event in the target stream would be deemed a 'hit' and a response to a masker event would be deemed a 'false alarm'.
source: A response to an event in the target stream would be deemed a 'hit' and a response to a masker event would be deemed a 'false alarm', allowing us to calculate d′ sensitivity for each of the three conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: Subjects were required to respond to brief color change flashes in the visual stimulus.
source: Subjects were also required to respond to brief color change flashes in the visual stimulus (Figure 1F)—this task was not difficult (overall hit rate was 87.7%), but ensured attentiveness to the visual stream.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: The overall hit rate for visual color change flashes was 87.7%.
source: Subjects were also required to respond to brief color change flashes in the visual stimulus (Figure 1F)—this task was not difficult (overall hit rate was 87.7%), but ensured attentiveness to the visual stream.
evidence: This is a data point from the experimental results.

claim: An improvement in behavioral performance in the match-target condition over the match-masker condition could only result from a benefit in separating the target and masker stream.
source: We reason that an improvement in behavioral performance in the match-target condition over the match-masker condition could only result from a benefit in separating the target and masker stream and thus be indicative of true, ongoing cross-modal binding, beyond a simple subjective report.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what the experimental results would indicate.

claim: For half of the subjects (N = 16), each auditory stream was an amplitude-modulated tone with fundamental frequency of 440 or 565 Hz.
source: For half of the subjects (N = 16), each auditory stream was an amplitude-modulated tone (fundamental frequency, F0, of 440 or 565 Hz, counterbalanced), and the events were 100 ms fluctuations in the carrier frequency of ±1.5 semitones (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: For the pitch task, the events were 100 ms fluctuations in the carrier frequency of ±1.5 semitones.
source: For half of the subjects (N = 16), each auditory stream was an amplitude-modulated tone (fundamental frequency, F0, of 440 or 565 Hz, counterbalanced), and the events were 100 ms fluctuations in the carrier frequency of ±1.5 semitones (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: For the other half of subjects (N = 16), each auditory stream was a band-pass filtered click train with a distinct pitch and timbre (synthetic vowels /u/ and /a/ with F0 of 175 and 195 Hz).
source: For the other half of subjects (N = 16), each auditory stream was a band-pass filtered click train with a distinct pitch and timbre (synthetic vowels /u/ and /a/; F0 of 175 and 195 Hz), and the events were small changes in the timbre of the stream generated by slightly modulating the first and second formant frequencies (F1 and F2, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: For the timbre task, the events were small changes in the timbre of the stream generated by slightly modulating the first and second formant frequencies.
source: For the other half of subjects (N = 16), each auditory stream was a band-pass filtered click train with a distinct pitch and timbre (synthetic vowels /u/ and /a/; F0 of 175 and 195 Hz), and the events were small changes in the timbre of the stream generated by slightly modulating the first and second formant frequencies (F1 and F2, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: There was a significant between-groups effect of event type on d′ sensitivity.
source: For d′, we found a significant between-groups effect of event type [F(1, 30) = 9.36, p = 0.0046, α = 0.05] and a significant within-subjects effect of coherence [F(2, 60) = 4.28, p = 0.018].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was a significant within-subjects effect of coherence on d′ sensitivity.
source: For d′, we found a significant between-groups effect of event type [F(1, 30) = 9.36, p = 0.0046, α = 0.05] and a significant within-subjects effect of coherence [F(2, 60) = 4.28, p = 0.018].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was no interaction between event type and coherence condition for d′ sensitivity.
source: There was no interaction between these two factors (p = 0.60), indicating the generality of the effect of cross-modal coherence on the selective attention task to different features and experimental setups, as well as different task difficulties (as performance was significantly better with pitch events vs timbre events).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The lack of interaction between event type and coherence condition indicates the generality of the effect of cross-modal coherence on the selective attention task.
source: There was no interaction between these two factors (p = 0.60), indicating the generality of the effect of cross-modal coherence on the selective attention task to different features and experimental setups, as well as different task difficulties (as performance was significantly better with pitch events vs timbre events).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical results.

claim: Performance was significantly better with pitch events vs timbre events.
source: There was no interaction between these two factors (p = 0.60), indicating the generality of the effect of cross-modal coherence on the selective attention task to different features and experimental setups, as well as different task difficulties (as performance was significantly better with pitch events vs timbre events).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Subjects performed better when the visual stimulus was coherent with the target auditory stream vs the auditory masker (match-target > match-masker).
source: Post hoc comparisons demonstrated that subjects performed better when the visual stimulus was coherent with the target auditory stream vs the auditory masker (match-target > match-masker; p = 0.0049, Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.017).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was a significant effect of event type on hit rate.
source: Similar results were obtained for hit rate: there was a significant effect of event type [F(1, 30) = 10.1, p = 0.0034] and also of visual coherence [F(2, 60) = 1.286, p = 0.0497].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was a significant effect of visual coherence on hit rate.
source: Similar results were obtained for hit rate: there was a significant effect of event type [F(1, 30) = 10.1, p = 0.0034] and also of visual coherence [F(2, 60) = 1.286, p = 0.0497].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was a significant difference between hit rate in the match-target and match-masker conditions.
source: Post hoc tests also showed a significant difference between hit rate in the match-target and match-masker conditions (p = 0.011).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: A visual stimulus can enhance a coherent auditory stimulus, even when that visual stimulus provides no useful visual information.
source: These results suggest that a visual stimulus can enhance a coherent auditory stimulus, even when that visual stimulus provides no useful visual information.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: There was no significant difference between the match-neither condition and either of the other two conditions.
source: There was no significant difference between the match-neither condition and either of the other two conditions.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was no significant effect of event type or coherence condition on bias.
source: For bias, there was no significant effect of event type or coherence condition (ANOVA as above, p = 0.284 and 0.985, respectively), and subjects were generally conservative in their responses (ln β > 0, intercept significant at F[1, 30] = 43.6, p < 0.0005).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Subjects were generally conservative in their responses (ln β > 0).
source: For bias, there was no significant effect of event type or coherence condition (ANOVA as above, p = 0.284 and 0.985, respectively), and subjects were generally conservative in their responses (ln β > 0, intercept significant at F[1, 30] = 43.6, p < 0.0005).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The lack of a variation in bias solidifies the notion that the observed pattern of responses results from changes in auditory detectability.
source: The lack of a variation in bias solidifies the notion that the observed pattern of responses results from changes in auditory detectability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical results.

claim: Neither event type nor coherence condition had a significant effect on false alarm rate.
source: Neither factor had a significant effect on false alarm rate (p = 0.29 and 0.18) or visual hit rate (p = 0.10 and 0.091).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Neither event type nor coherence condition had a significant effect on visual hit rate.
source: Neither factor had a significant effect on false alarm rate (p = 0.29 and 0.18) or visual hit rate (p = 0.10 and 0.091).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The temporal dynamics of one event or a repeating sequence are quite unlike many natural sounds, including speech.
source: However, the temporal dynamics of one event or a repeating sequence are quite unlike many natural sounds, including speech.
evidence: This is a statement based on general knowledge about natural sounds.

claim: Coherence discrimination was better for unpredictable sequences than for predictable ones.
source: A recent study addressed this by creating randomly timed sequences of discrete auditory-visual events, and showed that coherence discrimination was better for the unpredictable sequences than for predictable ones (Denison et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The noisy dynamics of stimulus features used in this study likely strengthened the bound percept.
source: Thus, the noisy dynamics of stimulus features used here not only allowed our stimuli to more closely emulate speech, but likely also strengthened the bound percept.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited research and the experimental design.

claim: The integration of visual and auditory information to create a cross-modal percept relies on the sensory signals being bound together.
source: The integration of visual and auditory information to create a cross-modal percept relies on the sensory signals being bound together.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in multisensory perception.

claim: The McGurk illusion can be reduced by contextually 'unbinding' the auditory and visual stimuli by preceding a test trial with non-matching audio and video.
source: The well-known McGurk illusion (McGurk and MacDonald, 1976) can be reduced by contextually 'unbinding' the auditory and visual stimuli by preceding a test trial with non-matching audio and video (Nahorna et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Illusory syllables are more likely when audio is paired with a dynamic face as opposed to a static image of a face.
source: Illusory syllables are also more likely when audio is paired with a dynamic face as opposed to a static image of a face that provides the same information regarding place of articulation (Rosenblum and Saldaña, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Individual differences in purely temporal processing are predictive of audio–visual fusion in multiple cross-modal illusions.
source: Additionally, individual differences in purely temporal processing (specifically, how long a discrete auditory event can lag a visual event and still be perceived as simultaneous) are predictive of audio–visual fusion in multiple cross-modal illusions (Stevenson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The present study is the only one to base a behavioral task on one auditory feature and use an orthogonal feature to create binding with the visual stimulus.
source: To our knowledge, the present study is the only one to base a behavioral task on one auditory feature and use an orthogonal feature to create binding with the visual stimulus, thus demonstrating an enhancement of an auditory feature about which the visual stimulus was uninformative.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study based on review of the literature.

claim: Temporal coherence between auditory features (i.e., pitch, timbre, location) is a principal contributor to the formation of auditory objects.
source: In the unimodal case, temporal coherence between auditory features (i.e., pitch, timbre, location) is a principal contributor to the formation of auditory objects (Shamma et al., 2011; Teki et al., 2013); however, the definition of an object can be difficult to pin down.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Griffiths and Warren (2004) suggest that incoming information corresponding to something in the sensory world is a criterion for what constitutes an auditory object.
source: Griffiths and Warren (2004) suggest criteria for what constitutes an auditory object. They first suggest that the incoming information corresponds to something in the sensory world; this often means a physical sound source, but they leave room in their definition for artificial sounds that could conceivably come from a real-world source.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Object-related information should be separable from other incoming sensory information.
source: Second, object-related information should be separable from other incoming sensory information—this was a major component of the present task.
evidence: This is a criterion from Griffiths and Warren (2004) applied to the present study.

claim: An object demonstrates perceptual invariance.
source: Third, an object demonstrates perceptual invariance. While this was not a focus of the present study, listeners' perceptions of the attended features were invariant in the face of fluctuating amplitude.
evidence: This is a criterion from Griffiths and Warren (2004) with an observation about the present study.

claim: An object is generalizable between senses.
source: The fourth and most interesting (in the context of the present discussion) criterion is that an object is generalizable between senses.
evidence: This is a criterion from Griffiths and Warren (2004).

claim: The sound-induced flash illusion is affected by audio–visual spatial congruence when observers are required to selectively attend to two spatially separated stimulus streams.
source: The sound-induced flash illusion (Shams et al., 2000, 2002), where the number of quick flashes perceived is strongly biased by the number of coincident beeps, is affected by audio–visual spatial congruence when observers are required to selectively attend to two spatially separated stimulus streams (Bizley et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cross-modal sensory interaction is strongest when evidence supports information from both modalities as originating from the same object.
source: This suggests that cross-modal sensory interaction is strongest when evidence supports information from both modalities as originating from the same object.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited research.

claim: There is evidence from unimodal studies that both visual and auditory attention operate on perceptual objects.
source: There is evidence from unimodal studies that both visual and auditory attention operate on perceptual objects, such that attention to one feature of an object enhances the perception of all its features (Alain and Arnott, 2000; Blaser et al., 2000; Shinn-Cunningham, 2008; Shamma et al., 2011; Maddox and Shinn-Cunningham, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Attention to one feature of an object enhances the perception of all its features.
source: There is evidence from unimodal studies that both visual and auditory attention operate on perceptual objects, such that attention to one feature of an object enhances the perception of all its features (Alain and Arnott, 2000; Blaser et al., 2000; Shinn-Cunningham, 2008; Shamma et al., 2011; Maddox and Shinn-Cunningham, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Processing of auditory pitch and timbre are enhanced when auditory amplitude is coherent with visual size.
source: Here, we show that processing of auditory pitch and timbre are enhanced when auditory amplitude is coherent with visual size.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: In the match-target condition, attention to the visual stimulus improves listening performance.
source: In the case of the match-target condition, this is beneficial, with attention to the visual stimulus improving listening performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Performance suffers in the match-masker case, where the incorrect auditory stream's features are enhanced through the same binding process.
source: Performance suffers in the match-masker case, where the incorrect auditory stream's features are enhanced through the same binding process.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Figure 3 shows a conceptual model of the processing underlying the experimental results.
source: Figure 3 shows a conceptual model of the processing underlying these results, using the pitch task as an example.
evidence: This refers to Figure 3 which presents a theoretical model.

claim: When there is cross-modal temporal coherence between a feature of an auditory and visual stream, those features are bound, resulting in a cross-modal object.
source: When there is cross-modal temporal coherence between a feature of an auditory and visual stream, those features are bound. This results in a cross-modal object (just as two auditory or visual streams with the same envelope very likely would have bound together as well).
evidence: This is part of the conceptual model proposed by the authors.

claim: One possibility for biological implementation is that cross-modal coherence enables neural activity patterns in visual cortex to reinforce the activity elicited by the coherent auditory stream in auditory cortex.
source: How this model might be biologically implemented remains to be elucidated, but one possibility is that cross-modal coherence between stimulus modalities enables neural activity patterns in visual cortex to reinforce the activity elicited by the coherent auditory stream in auditory cortex (Ghazanfar and Schroeder, 2006; Bizley and King, 2012).
evidence: This is speculation about neural mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: If the formation of cross-modal objects underlies the present results, then the enhancement should be bidirectional.
source: If the formation of cross-modal objects underlies the present results, then the enhancement should be bidirectional.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.

claim: The visual stimulus features should be enhanced when it is coherent with any auditory stimulus compared to when it is not.
source: Since there was only one visual stimulus (i.e., no competing distractor visual stimulus), its features should be enhanced when it is coherent with any auditory stimulus compared to when it is not, but further experiments specifically designed to test this bi-directionality are needed.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model, with acknowledgment that it needs testing.

claim: Within one modality, a stream or object can be thought of as occupying a point or region of a multidimensional feature space.
source: Within one modality, a stream or object can be thought of as occupying a point or region of a multidimensional feature space: it can have a specific pitch, location, onset or offset time, etc that define it (Shamma et al., 2011; Teki et al., 2011, 2013; Micheyl et al., 2013; Christiansen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: Two streams may bind if they are close together in one or more dimensions of feature space.
source: Two streams may bind if they are close together in one or more of these dimensions, such as tones of two frequencies that start and stop at the same time (Shamma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a principle of auditory scene analysis supported by citation.

claim: Similar principles should govern the formation of cross-modal objects, with the caveat that only some stimulus features span sensory boundaries.
source: Similar principles should govern the formation of cross-modal objects, with the caveat that only some stimulus features span sensory boundaries.
evidence: This is an inference extending unimodal principles to cross-modal perception.

claim: Time and space are physical dimensions that span sensory boundaries for audio-visual stimuli.
source: These dimensions could be physical, such as time and space for audio-visual stimuli (Alais and Burr, 2004; Talsma et al., 2010; Bizley et al., 2012), or learned statistical correspondences, such as the linguistic connection between an image of someone with protruded lips and an auditory /u/ vowel.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Learned statistical correspondences, such as the linguistic connection between an image of someone with protruded lips and an auditory /u/ vowel, can be dimensions that span sensory boundaries.
source: These dimensions could be physical, such as time and space for audio-visual stimuli (Alais and Burr, 2004; Talsma et al., 2010; Bizley et al., 2012), or learned statistical correspondences, such as the linguistic connection between an image of someone with protruded lips and an auditory /u/ vowel.
evidence: This is an example based on knowledge of speech perception.

claim: Within a cross-modal object, all features are enhanced and disagreements or ambiguities are resolved.
source: Within this object, all features are enhanced and disagreements or ambiguities are resolved, either by letting the more reliable modality dominate (typically vision for space, audition for timing [Talsma et al., 2010]), or by creating an intermediary percept (e.g., the McGurk effect).
evidence: This is a principle of multisensory integration supported by citation and examples.

claim: Vision typically dominates for spatial information and audition for temporal information in multisensory integration.
source: Within this object, all features are enhanced and disagreements or ambiguities are resolved, either by letting the more reliable modality dominate (typically vision for space, audition for timing [Talsma et al., 2010]), or by creating an intermediary percept (e.g., the McGurk effect).
evidence: This is established knowledge in multisensory perception, supported by citation.

claim: The demonstration of feature enhancement within a putative object is the marker of binding.
source: How does one establish that cross-modal binding has occurred? Here, we suggest that the demonstration of feature enhancement within a putative object is the marker of binding.
evidence: This is a methodological claim proposed by the authors.

claim: Attending to the color of a visual stream enhanced the perception of the pitch or timbre of an auditory stream, despite those features being unrelated.
source: We showed that attending to the color of a visual stream enhanced the perception of the pitch or timbre of an auditory stream, despite the fact that those two (i.e., color and pitch or color and timbre) features on their own were unrelated.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: This is the first example of a continuous visual signal benefitting listening abilities through enhanced auditory scene segregation.
source: This influence instead occurred through a chain of bound features within a cross-modal object, with a shared temporal trajectory linking visual size and auditory amplitude and is, to our knowledge, the first example of a continuous visual signal benefitting listening abilities through enhanced auditory scene segregation.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on review of the literature.

claim: Subjects gave written informed consent and were paid for their participation.
source: Subjects gave written informed consent and were paid for their participation.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental procedures.

claim: Subjects had normal hearing (audiologic thresholds ≤20 dB hearing loss at octave frequencies from 250 to 8000 Hz).
source: Subjects had normal hearing (audiologic thresholds ≤20 dB hearing loss at octave frequencies from 250 to 8000 Hz) and normal or corrected visual acuity.
evidence: This is a description of the subject inclusion criteria.

claim: Subjects had normal or corrected visual acuity.
source: Subjects had normal hearing (audiologic thresholds ≤20 dB hearing loss at octave frequencies from 250 to 8000 Hz) and normal or corrected visual acuity.
evidence: This is a description of the subject inclusion criteria.

claim: A total of 32 subjects participated (17 male, age 18–33 years).
source: A total of 32 subjects participated (17 male, age 18–33 years).
evidence: This is demographic information about the study participants.

claim: The pitch task was run at the University of Washington in the lab of AKCL.
source: The pitch task was run at the University of Washington in the lab of AKCL.
evidence: This is information about where the experiment was conducted.

claim: The timbre task was performed at the University College London in the lab of JKB.
source: The timbre task was performed at the University College London in the lab of JKB.
evidence: This is information about where the experiment was conducted.

claim: Envelopes for visual envelope and auditory amplitude were created using frequency domain synthesis.
source: Envelopes for visual envelope and auditory amplitude were created using the same frequency domain synthesis.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus generation methods.

claim: Visual envelopes were created by subsampling the auditory envelope at the monitor frame-rate of 60 Hz.
source: Visual envelopes were created by subsampling the auditory envelope at the monitor frame-rate of 60 Hz, starting with the first auditory sample, so that auditory amplitude corresponded with the disc radius at the beginning of each frame.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus generation methods.

claim: Stimuli were presented in an unlit sound-attenuating room over earphones.
source: Stimuli were presented in an unlit sound-attenuating room over earphones.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: All auditory stimuli were presented diotically.
source: All stimuli were presented diotically.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus presentation method.

claim: Gray discs subtended between 1° and 2.5° at 50 cm viewing distance.
source: Gray discs subtended between 1° and 2.5° at 50 cm viewing distance.
evidence: This is a description of the visual stimulus parameters.

claim: The white ring extended 0.125° beyond the gray disc.
source: The white ring extended 0.125° beyond the gray disc.
evidence: This is a description of the visual stimulus parameters.

claim: The auditory masker began 1 s after the target auditory stimulus.
source: They began with only the target auditory stimulus and the visual stimulus, indicating the to-be-attended auditory stream to the subject. The auditory masker began 1 s later.
evidence: This is a description of the trial structure.

claim: Events did not occur in the first 2 s or the last 1 s of each trial, or within 1.2 s of any other events in either modality.
source: Events did not occur in the first 2 s (1 s after the masker began) or the last 1 s of each trial, or within 1.2 s of any other events in either modality.
evidence: This is a description of the event timing constraints.

claim: A response made within 1 s following an event was attributed to that event.
source: A response made within 1 s following an event was attributed to that event.
evidence: This is a description of the response analysis method.

claim: An event in either auditory stream or the visual stream could only begin when both auditory envelopes were above 75% maximum.
source: To ensure audibility and equivalent target to masker ratios without providing confounding information to the subject, an event in either auditory stream or the visual stream could only begin when both auditory envelopes were above 75% maximum.
evidence: This is a description of the event timing constraints and their rationale.

claim: There were between 1 and 3 inclusive (mean 2) events in both the target and masker in each trial.
source: There were between 1 and 3 inclusive (mean 2) events in both the target and masker in each trial.
evidence: This is a description of the trial structure.

claim: There were between 0 and 2 inclusive (mean 1) visual flashes per trial.
source: There were also between 0 and 2 inclusive (mean 1) visual flashes per trial, in which the outer ring changed from white to cyan (0% red, 100% blue, 100% green) and back.
evidence: This is a description of the trial structure.

claim: Each subject completed 32 trials of each stimulus condition (96 total).
source: Each subject completed 32 trials of each stimulus condition (96 total), leading to 64 potential hits and 64 potential false alarms for each condition (i.e., 128 responses considered for each d′ calculation) as well as 32 visual flashes per condition.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: When computing d′, auditory hit and false alarm rates were calculated by adding 0.5 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator so that d′ had finite limits.
source: When computing d′, auditory hit and false alarm rates were calculated by adding 0.5 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator so that d′ had finite limits.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: Subjects were seated 50 cm from the screen in the pitch task.
source: Subjects were seated 50 cm from the screen.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup for the pitch task.

claim: Each auditory stream in the pitch task was presented at an average of 66 or 63 dB SPL in 42 dB SPL white noise.
source: Each auditory stream was an amplitude-modulated sinusoid with a frequency of either 440 or 565 Hz and was presented at an average of 66 or 63 dB sound pressure level (SPL), respectively in 42 dB SPL white noise to mask any residual sound from outside the sound-treated booth.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus parameters for the pitch task.

claim: The higher frequency stream was attenuated 3 dB so that both streams were of equivalent perceived loudness.
source: The higher frequency stream was more salient in piloting and so was attenuated 3 dB so that both streams were of equivalent perceived loudness.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus calibration procedure.

claim: Subjects were seated 60 cm from the screen with their heads held stationary by a chinrest in the timbre task.
source: Subjects were seated 60 cm from the screen with their heads held stationary by a chinrest.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup for the timbre task.

claim: Streams in the timbre task were calibrated to be 65 dB SPL and presented against 54 dB SPL background noise.
source: Streams were calibrated to be 65 dB SPL (RMS normalized) using an artificial ear (Brüel & Kjær, Nærum, Denmark) and presented against a low level of background noise (54 dB SPL).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus parameters for the timbre task.

claim: Before testing, subjects in the timbre task completed a threshold task to determine the size of timbre shift that resulted in 70% detection.
source: Before testing, subjects completed a threshold task to determine the size of timbre shift that resulted in 70% detection.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for the timbre task.

claim: The average perturbation in the timbre task was 12.25% of distance from steady-state vowel to deviant vowel in the F1–F2 plane.
source: The average perturbation (as percentage of distance from steady-state vowel to deviant vowel in the F1–F2 plane) was 12.25%.
evidence: This is a data point from the timbre task threshold procedure.

claim: Four subjects out of twenty tested did not perform well enough to be included (d′ < 0.7) in the timbre task.
source: Four subjects out of twenty tested did not perform well enough to be included (d′ < 0.7), leading to the final N = 16 analyzed.
evidence: This is information about subject exclusion criteria.
